paths.title: Authorization, Ownership & Multi-Tenancy
paths.description: Enforce object, action, role, policy, tenant, field, and administrative permissions independently from authentication and client UI state.
topics: Object-level authorization
Every request that references an object identifier must verify that the current principal may act on that specific object.
Load objects through authorization-aware queries or policy checks and test cross-user identifier substitution explicitly.
Function-level authorization
A user may have access to some routes or commands but not privileged administrative or destructive operations.
Declare required capabilities per action and default to deny when no policy grants the operation.
Role-based access control
RBAC assigns permissions through roles and works well when organizational responsibilities map cleanly to stable capability groups.
Keep role definitions centralized and authorize capabilities rather than scattering role-name comparisons throughout handlers.
Attribute-based policy
ABAC evaluates properties of the principal, resource, action, and environment for more contextual decisions.
Keep policy inputs explicit and auditable, and avoid embedding opaque policy conditions inside unrelated business code.
Ownership checks
Ownership is one authorization relationship but may not cover teams, delegated access, shared resources, or administrative duties.
Model ownership and sharing explicitly and test every alternate relationship rather than comparing only user IDs.
Tenant isolation
Multi-tenant systems must prevent one tenant from reading, modifying, searching, caching, or exporting another tenant's data.
Carry a trusted tenant identifier from authenticated context into every storage query and make missing tenant scope fail closed.
Field-level authorization
A principal can be allowed to read an object while some fields remain sensitive or immutable.
Construct response and update DTOs from allowlisted fields based on policy rather than serializing whole records automatically.
Permission caching
Caching authorization results can improve latency but stale policy or membership changes can create dangerous access windows.
Cache only when revocation/freshness requirements are defined and include policy version or identity context in cache keys.
Administrative access
Support and operations staff often need elevated access that creates significant insider and account-compromise risk.
Use least privilege, stronger authentication, just-in-time elevation, audit trails, and clear purpose limitations for administrative actions.
Authorization testing
Happy-path permission tests miss the cross-object and cross-role cases attackers actually exploit.
Build a permission matrix and automate negative tests for wrong user, wrong tenant, missing role, altered field, and direct object ID access.

paths.title: API Security & Abuse Resistance
paths.description: Address object authorization, authentication, resource consumption, sensitive workflows, SSRF, misconfiguration, inventory, unsafe upstream APIs, injection, and abuse controls.
topics: Broken object authorization
Predictable IDs become dangerous when APIs authorize only the route or user session and not the referenced object.
Check object-level permission in every function that uses client-controlled identifiers to access data.
Broken authentication
Weak credential, token, session, reset, or verification flows can compromise the identity layer for the entire API.
Use vetted authentication mechanisms, strong session management, monitoring, and tests for bypass and recovery paths.
Property-level authorization
Mass assignment and excessive data exposure occur when clients can read or change fields beyond their permissions.
Allowlist readable and writable fields explicitly and validate output schemas as well as input schemas.
Resource consumption
Expensive queries, huge bodies, unbounded pagination, file processing, or repeated work can exhaust CPU, memory, storage, or third-party quotas.
Set endpoint-specific size, count, complexity, concurrency, and time limits and monitor rejected usage.
Sensitive business flows
Ticket buying, signup, messaging, coupon redemption, and similar workflows can be abused even by authenticated users making valid requests.
Model abuse limits around business impact, identity, velocity, inventory, and automation resistance rather than only IP rate limits.
Server-side request forgery
Fetching client-controlled URLs can expose internal services, cloud metadata, credentials, or privileged network locations.
Allowlist destinations or protocols, resolve and validate addresses carefully, restrict egress, and limit redirects, response size, and time.
Security misconfiguration
Debug endpoints, permissive CORS, default credentials, verbose errors, unsafe headers, or exposed admin tools create avoidable attack surface.
Use hardened environment-specific configuration, automated checks, and minimal exposed services.
API inventory
Unknown, deprecated, test, or undocumented endpoints often escape normal patching and authorization review.
Maintain an inventory of deployed APIs, versions, owners, data sensitivity, and retirement dates, and remove obsolete routes.
Unsafe upstream consumption
Data from partner or third-party APIs remains untrusted and may contain malicious redirects, payloads, sizes, or identifiers.
Apply TLS, timeouts, response limits, schema validation, redirect policy, and output encoding to upstream data just as you would to client input.
Injection defenses
SQL, command, template, LDAP, and other injections occur when data becomes executable syntax in an interpreter.
Use parameterized APIs and safe library primitives, validate structure, and avoid shell or query string concatenation with untrusted values.

paths.title: Configuration, Secrets, TLS & Security Headers
paths.description: Manage environment configuration, secret lifecycle, encryption keys, TLS termination, proxy trust, CORS, security headers, and credential rotation safely.
topics: Configuration validation
Missing or malformed runtime configuration should fail during startup rather than producing partially broken live behavior.
Parse environment configuration into a typed validated object once and reject invalid combinations before opening the server port.
Secret separation
Passwords, API keys, private keys, and signing material require different handling from ordinary configuration.
Inject secrets from a managed secret system, exclude them from source and images, and minimize which process roles can read them.
Secret rotation
Long-lived static credentials increase the impact window after accidental disclosure or compromise.
Use short-lived credentials where possible and design services to reload or roll credentials without an outage.
Encryption key management
Encrypted data is only as secure and recoverable as the lifecycle, access, backup, and rotation of its keys.
Use managed key systems where appropriate and separate key permissions from application data permissions.
TLS termination
TLS can terminate at a load balancer, reverse proxy, service mesh, or application, affecting how the backend determines scheme and client properties.
Document the termination point and trust only proxy-provided protocol or client headers from explicitly trusted hops.
Certificate validation
Backend clients must validate server certificates and hostnames rather than disabling TLS checks to fix local connectivity issues.
Use a trusted CA model and provide development certificates or explicit trust stores instead of setting insecure global bypass flags.
CORS policy
CORS controls whether browser scripts from other origins may read responses; it does not protect APIs from non-browser callers.
Allow only required origins, methods, and headers and do not combine wildcard origins with credentialed cross-origin access.
Security headers
Headers such as Content-Security-Policy, frame-ancestors, HSTS, Referrer-Policy, and nosniff reduce browser attack surface.
Set them centrally, test them in deployment, and tune policies from actual application requirements rather than copying incompatible templates.
Proxy trust
Framework settings that trust forwarding headers can let clients spoof IP, host, or scheme when configured for more proxies than actually exist.
Configure the exact trusted proxy topology and test direct-to-app requests if bypassing the proxy is technically possible.
Secret-safe logging
Configuration dumps and error objects can contain tokens, connection strings, cookies, or authorization headers.
Redact known secret fields and headers before structured logging and avoid logging full environment objects or raw requests.

paths.title: Background Jobs, Queues & Scheduling
paths.description: Move durable asynchronous work into queues with explicit delivery semantics, idempotency, retries, dead letters, concurrency, scheduling, and observability.
topics: Async work boundary
Email, media processing, reports, webhooks, and long workflows often should not extend the latency or failure surface of an HTTP request.
Persist the intent and enqueue durable work after the authoritative state change instead of starting fire-and-forget promises in request handlers.
Delivery semantics
Queues may deliver at least once, at most once, or with provider-specific guarantees, so consumers must understand possible duplication and loss.
Design consumers around the queue's real delivery model and make duplicate processing safe when at-least-once delivery is possible.
Idempotent consumers
A retried message can otherwise send duplicate emails, charge twice, or create repeated records.
Use stable job IDs, processed-event records, unique constraints, or domain idempotency keys around side effects.
Retry policy
Immediate unlimited retry amplifies outages and can overwhelm a failing dependency.
Classify transient versus permanent errors, use bounded exponential backoff with jitter, and stop retrying invalid inputs.
Dead-letter handling
Messages that repeatedly fail need a quarantine and recovery workflow instead of silently disappearing or blocking the queue.
Send exhausted jobs to a dead-letter store with failure context, alert ownership, and an explicit replay procedure.
Consumer concurrency
More workers increase throughput only until downstream databases, APIs, CPU, or rate limits become saturated.
Set concurrency from measured service capacity and use queue depth/age plus downstream health as scaling signals.
Job ordering
Some workflows require per-entity ordering while global ordering can unnecessarily serialize unrelated work.
Partition or key jobs by the smallest domain boundary that requires order and make cross-key ordering assumptions explicit.
Scheduled jobs
Cron-like schedules can run twice during failover or be missed during downtime depending on the platform.
Make scheduled work idempotent, store last-success markers when necessary, and prefer durable schedulers for business-critical deadlines.
Transactional outbox
Writing business state and publishing an event separately can create a gap where one succeeds and the other fails.
Write an outbox record in the same database transaction, then publish and mark it delivered asynchronously.
Queue observability
Queue length alone hides old stuck jobs, retry storms, poison messages, and per-type bottlenecks.
Monitor oldest message age, attempts, failures, processing latency, throughput, dead letters, and downstream saturation by job type.

paths.title: Streams, Files & Upload Processing
paths.description: Handle request bodies, large downloads, multipart uploads, storage, backpressure, validation, antivirus/media processing, and secure file lifecycle without exhausting memory.
topics: Streaming bodies
Large HTTP bodies can arrive incrementally and should not always be buffered into one in-memory object.
Stream suitable payloads and enforce byte limits while reading so oversized requests are rejected before memory is exhausted.
Backpressure
A fast producer can overwhelm a slower file, network, compression, or transform consumer if flow control is ignored.
Use pipeline-style streaming primitives that propagate backpressure and errors across the complete chain.
Multipart uploads
Multipart forms mix metadata and file parts with boundaries and require streaming parsers designed for hostile input.
Use a maintained parser, limit part count/size, and never trust client filenames, MIME types, or extensions as validation.
File-type validation
Extensions and Content-Type headers are attacker-controlled and do not prove the actual file format.
Validate signatures/content where risk warrants it and process uploads in isolated tooling when parsers handle complex formats.
Upload naming
User filenames can contain traversal sequences, control characters, collisions, or unsafe display content.
Generate server-owned storage keys and keep the original display name as separately escaped metadata if needed.
Direct-to-object-storage uploads
Signed upload URLs can keep large bytes away from application servers but shift validation and lifecycle steps.
Authorize the upload intent first, constrain key/size/type metadata where supported, and verify the completed object before publishing it.
Download authorization
Guessable object URLs can bypass application authorization when storage is public by default.
Keep sensitive objects private and issue short-lived signed downloads only after server-side permission checks.
Archive extraction
ZIP and archive files can contain path traversal, huge expanded sizes, nested archives, or malicious entries.
Limit file count and expanded bytes, normalize extraction paths, and isolate extraction from privileged filesystems.
Media processing
Image, PDF, audio, and video parsers have significant CPU and security exposure and may process attacker-controlled inputs.
Run expensive transformations asynchronously with time/memory limits and keep processors patched and isolated.
File retention
Uploads create long-lived storage, privacy, backup, and deletion obligations beyond the initial request.
Define lifecycle states, retention, orphan cleanup, legal/privacy deletion behavior, and storage observability for every file class.
codeExamples:
import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
await pipeline(request, byteLimitTransform(10 * 1024 * 1024), objectStore.createWriteStream(objectKey));
